sources.title: Human History Map, historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Repository index entry for exact id dutch-east-indies-1920: name Dutch East Indies, circa 1920 to 1938. Related ids were audited separately; this source supplies atlas metadata only.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1920 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact-id 1920 to 1930 MultiPolygon: 15 polygons/rings, 908 positions, bbox 95.1903519 E to 140.9612096 E and 10.3776059 S to 5.5702130 N. Geometry is a locator, not verified sovereignty or an island inventory.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1930 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact-id 1930 to 1938 MultiPolygon. Its 15 rings, 908 positions and coordinates are identical to the 1920 snapshot.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1938 historical basemap topology
sources.note: The same archipelago geometry continues for 1938 to 1945 but is reassigned to civ netherlands-1878 with label Dutch East Indies. This proves the exact-id cutoff is a data handoff, not the colony’s fall.

sources.title: Indisch Herinneringscentrum, Ons Land: the Netherlands | the Dutch East Indies | Indonesia
sources.note: English educational booklet, printed pp. 38 to 39: 1918 Volksraad composition and advisory power; higher education, 1926 to 1927 uprisings and repression, PNI, Youth Pledge, arrests/exile and rejection of the Soetardjo petition. It is a timeline, so claims are paired with specialist studies where needed.

sources.title: Indisch Herinneringscentrum, prewar political and military developments
sources.note: “Rulers,” “Ethical policy” and “Nationalism” sections: diverse earlier authorities, Dutch dependence on Indigenous officials, gradual openings in education/administration, and the growth and repression of Indonesian nationalism around 1920 to 1930.

sources.title: The Colonial State: Violence and Modernity, Resistance and Repression
sources.note: Open-access chapter in MERDEKA, printed pp. 20 to 21 and 36 to 38: Ethical Policy’s paternalism and colonial uses of education, irrigation and migration; racial law, constrained representative politics and the 1936 to 1938 Soetardjo petition.

sources.title: Two Sides of the Same Coin: Direct Taxation and Negotiated Governance in Colonial Indonesia
sources.note: Journal of Social History, Fairness and Equality and Centralization and Unification sections, especially text lines 93 to 104 in the web edition: racialized sociolegal classes, separate legal systems, uneven local taxation and the 1920 unified income tax.

sources.title: Boven Digoel: Projecting a New Society
sources.note: Southeast Asian Studies 14(1), abstract and pp. 87 to 90: the camp followed the 1926 to 1927 revolts, removed political prisoners from their communities, subjected them to surveillance and “re-education,” and became a censorship-shaped warning image.

sources.title: Bahaja Menghantjam: Ups and Downs of the New PNI Movement 1931 to 1942
sources.note: Indonesian Historical Studies 5(2), abstract and “Vergader Verbod and Arrest” section: repression, the 1 August 1933 assembly ban, secret small meetings, arrests, underground reorganization and cadre education.

sources.title: Ons Land, Soetardjo Petition
sources.note: Event record dated 29 September 1936 to 16 November 1938: petition requested a conference and plan for a self-governing position within the kingdom; the Dutch government rejected it in 1938, frustrating moderate nationalists.

sources.title: Urban Java during the Depression
sources.note: Journal of Southeast Asian Studies abstract/extract: export earnings collapse, wage cuts, unemployment and casual work in Java’s towns; some migrants returned to villages and relied on relatives. The evidence is urban Java, not the whole archipelago.

sources.title: Education, Labour, and Discipline: Indigenous Children in Colonial Asia
sources.note: International Review of Social History, “Expenditure on colonial education” section: villagers bore much school cost; less than one quarter of Indigenous children were enrolled in primary school in the 1930s; spending favored European-status and ethnic Chinese schools.

sources.title: Institut Teknologi Bandung, History
sources.note: Official university history: technical college founded 3 July 1920 with one faculty and water/road engineering major; 28 students in 1920 to 1921, only two Indonesian; four Indonesian students among the 1926 engineering graduates.

sources.title: Directorate General of Culture, the Among system at Taman Siswa
sources.note: Official Indonesian culture page: Taman Siswa opened 3 July 1922; the Among approach rejected coercion, treated teachers as guides, described developmental stages and argued education should not be reserved for elites.

sources.title: Directorate General of Culture, Dalem Jayadipuran and the First Indonesian Women’s Congress
sources.note: Official heritage page, section on 22 to 25 December 1928: seven initiating organizations, thirty women’s organizations and about 700 participants met to coordinate work for women and society.

sources.title: Arsip Nasional Republik Indonesia, Arsip sebagai Simpul Pemersatu Bangsa
sources.note: ANRI archival journal, PDF pp. 4 to 5: transcription of the 27 to 28 October 1928 youth congress decision in period spelling, including “KAMI POETRA DAN POETRI INDONESIA” and the language pledge.

sources.title: Directorate General of Culture, the story behind Indonesia Raya
sources.note: Official culture page: journalist and musician W. R. Soepratman played Indonesia Raya without lyrics at the Second Youth Congress on 28 October 1928 to reduce risk of colonial repression.

sources.title: Grammar of Difference? Dutch Colonial Labour Policies and Social Norms on Work and Gender
sources.note: International Review of Social History, discussion around Table 3: 1930 Java/Madura census recorded occupations for nearly 30% of married women, especially agriculture, food/textile work and retail, while excluding much subsistence and communal labor.

sources.title: The Price of Un/Freedom: Indonesia’s Colonial and Contemporary Plantation Labor Regimes
sources.note: Comparative Studies in Society and History, “Tobacco and Rubber” section: Sumatran tobacco, rubber and early oil palm; migrant Chinese and Javanese workers; coercive contracts and penal sanctions; desertion and later shifts toward casual labor.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Traditional Settlement at Nagari Sijunjung
sources.note: Indonesia’s 2015 tentative-list nomination: 76 rumah gadang of nine clans, female-line descent and inheritance, matrilocal marriage, clan leadership, customary teaching, mosques, madrasah, fields and markets. Used as continuity evidence for one Minangkabau setting, not direct 1920 census data.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Javanese Shoulder Cloth (22.167.1)
sources.note: Object record: cotton central-Javanese batik, mid-nineteenth to early twentieth century; indigo/white ceplok pattern; historical association of patterns with social status and court restrictions that loosened over time.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Warung with food displayed on a table in inland Java
sources.note: Public-domain stereograph RP-F-2001-17-184, attributed to Neville Keasberry, Java/Malang possibly, dated broadly 1900 to 1935. Caption identifies a warung with food displayed; it does not identify dishes or customers.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Album leaf with the interior of a house in Tjimahi
sources.note: Album leaf RP-F-2012-19-45-5(R), dated 1920 to 1927, twelve photographs mainly of a Tjimahi home in 1925; annotations identify front gallery, carpet/no carpet and dining room. Album belonged to a Dutch family.

sources.title: The expansion of medical education in the Dutch East Indies and the Indonesian medical profession
sources.note: Medical History 68 (2024), “Improvements,” “Medical students” and “Further improvements”: STOVIA/NIAS, 1925 Public Health Service, 1927 Batavia Medical School, bursary-service obligations, discrimination and small but consequential Indonesian physician cohort.

sources.title: Species sanitation of malaria in the Netherlands East Indies (1913 to 1942)
sources.note: PubMed historical-article abstract: 1920s “species sanitation” targeted species-specific Anopheles breeding places, but effectiveness depended on biological, technical, economic, social and political conditions and remained limited to local exceptions.

sources.title: (Post)Colonial Pipes: Urban Water Supply in Colonial and Contemporary Jakarta
sources.note: Library of Congress-hosted open book PDF, chapter pp. 63 to 86, especially printed pp. 65, 78 to 79: 1929 household flow figures, European residents’ disproportionate consumption, public hydrants and the 1926 paid water-delivery system in Batavia/Jakarta.

sources.title: Modernization of the Indonesian City, 1920 to 1960
sources.note: Open-access introductory chapter, printed pp. 5 to 7: colonial reformers defined kampongs by supposed lacks such as pipes, sanitation, washing places and water closets, often in contemptuous language; urban improvement also protected unequal colonial order.

sources.title: The Rijksmuseum Bulletin, colonial archaeology and Candi Panataran
sources.note: Rijksmuseum Bulletin article, printed p. 266: Archaeological Service restoration shifted under F. D. K. Bosch, beginning with Candi Panataran in 1918; local Javanese dignitaries joined an advisory committee and results were presented to students and teachers; Depression cuts halted most reconstruction.

sources.title: Bosscha Observatory, History and Profile
sources.note: Official observatory history: astronomy society formed in Bandung in 1920 to build and maintain an observatory; Bosscha funded major equipment; observatory inaugurated 1 January 1923 and transferred to the Indonesian government in 1951.

sources.title: Nature (1932), Early Man in Java
sources.note: Contemporary Nature notice dated 11 June 1932: C. ter Haar’s Ngandong discovery and the Geological Survey report on braincase remains from a Solo River bone bed. The period classification and estimated age are historical, not accepted uncritically.

sources.title: Smithsonian, Indonesia’s Top Five Hominid Fossil Sites
sources.note: Smithsonian science overview, Ngandong and Mojokerto sections: 1930s finds are now classified as Homo erectus; later fieldwork revised age estimates, and the 1936 Mojokerto child skull’s exact find location has been questioned.

sources.title: Indisch Herinneringscentrum, the road to Japanese occupation
sources.note: “Invasion” and “Indies government” sections: Japan took Tarakan in January 1942, landed on Java on 1 March after the Java Sea defeat, and the colonial government relocated to Australia.

sources.title: Nationaal Archief, Transfer of sovereignty to Indonesia (1949)
sources.note: Dutch National Archives education source: Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945; the Netherlands refused, war followed, and sovereignty was transferred on 27 December 1949. The page’s New Guinea references and linked archive context show western New Guinea initially stayed under Dutch administration; it also records the Netherlands’ 2023 unqualified recognition of the 1945 date.

proposedOverrides.summary: The late Dutch East Indies: unequal colonial rule, Indonesian organizing, family and working life, schools, science, medicine, water and the atlas’s false 1938 endpoint.

batchIdentityNotes: Targeted only exact id dutch-east-indies-1920. The index says Dutch East Indies, circa 1920 to 1938, and coverage showed card null before integration. No appliesTo field is proposed.

The exact id has two consecutive intervals, 1920 to 1930 and 1930 to 1938. Both decode to the identical 15-polygon, 15-ring, 908-position MultiPolygon with bbox 95.19035190351906 E to 140.96120961209613 E and 10.377605908264307 S to 5.570212981647892 N.

The same geometry appears before 1920 under netherlands-1878 and netherlands-indies, and after 1938 under netherlands-1878 with label Dutch East Indies. Thus 1920 and 1938 are importer identity changes, not the colony’s founding or fall.

Related records were kept separate: dutch-east-indies (1650 to 1878) and indonesia (1945 to ) already have cards; netherlands-indies (1914 to 1920) remains a distinct missing record. No alias association or successor edge is added.

The imported geometry broadly covers the claimed Dutch archipelago from Sumatra to western New Guinea and excludes Portuguese Timor. It is a locator only: its 15 rings omit many islands, simplified coasts cause false-negative city containment tests, and it cannot verify control, ethnicity or daily-life uniformity.

At 1945 the atlas splits western New Guinea into a separate Dutch Guinea feature and assigns most of the rest to Indonesia. That geometry change is an atlas handoff, not a claim that every sovereignty question was settled in 1945.
